claim: Mice with ablation of Epithelial splicing regulatory protein (Esrp1) develop cleft lip and palate.
source: Mice with ablation of Epithelial splicing regulatory protein (Esrp1) develop cleft lip and palate.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by experimental data from Esrp1 knockout mice showing fully penetrant bilateral cleft lip and palate.

claim: Loss of both Esrp1 and its paralog Esrp2 results in widespread developmental defects with broad implications to human disease.
source: Loss of both Esrp1 and its paralog Esrp2 results in widespread developmental defects with broad implications to human disease.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing multiple organ defects in double knockout mice.

claim: Deletion of the Esrps in the epidermis revealed their requirement for establishing a proper skin barrier.
source: Deletion of the Esrps in the epidermis revealed their requirement for establishing a proper skin barrier, a primary function of epithelial cells comprising the epidermis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from conditional knockout mice showing skin barrier defects measured by water loss assay.

claim: Over 95% of multi-exon genes in humans are alternatively spliced.
source: Indeed, over 95% of multi-exon genes in humans are alternatively spliced and AS has been shown to have essential functions across vertebrate and invertebrate lineages (Graveley, 2001; Pan et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Alternative splicing has been shown to have essential functions across vertebrate and invertebrate lineages.
source: Indeed, over 95% of multi-exon genes in humans are alternatively spliced and AS has been shown to have essential functions across vertebrate and invertebrate lineages (Graveley, 2001; Pan et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The mutually exclusive AS of exons IIIb and IIIc alters the second half of the Immunoglobulin-like III (Ig3) domain of the receptor extracellular ligand binding domain.
source: The mutually exclusive AS of exons IIIb and IIIc alters the second half of the Immunoglobulin-like III (Ig3) domain of the receptor extracellular ligand binding domain, and in turn alters the binding specificity of the Fgfr2 receptor to its cognate Fgf ligands (Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Knockout of Fgfr2-IIIb or one of its primary ligands, Fgf10, in mouse results in developmental defects in limb, lung, craniofacial and palate formation, salivary gland, tooth, and epidermal appendage (hair) formation.
source: Knockout (KO) of Fgfr2-IIIb or one of its primary ligands, Fgf10, in mouse results in developmental defects in limb, lung, craniofacial and palate formation, salivary gland, tooth, and epidermal appendage (hair) formation (Xu et al., 1998; De Moerlooze et al., 2000; Ohuchi et al., 2000; Revest et al., 2001; Petiot et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The ESRPs (ESRP1 and ESRP2) expression is epithelial cell type-specific.
source: The expression of the ESRPs (ESRP1 and ESRP2) is epithelial cell type-specific and knockdown of ESRP1 and ESRP2 in epithelial cells induces a complete switch from Fgfr2-IIIb to Fgfr2-IIIc isoforms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study and previous work by the authors.

claim: Knockdown of ESRP1 and ESRP2 in epithelial cells induces a complete switch from Fgfr2-IIIb to Fgfr2-IIIc isoforms.
source: The expression of the ESRPs (ESRP1 and ESRP2) is epithelial cell type-specific and knockdown of ESRP1 and ESRP2 in epithelial cells induces a complete switch from Fgfr2-IIIb to Fgfr2-IIIc isoforms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from previous work by the authors.

claim: Ectopic expression of Esrp1 in mesenchymal cells induces a switch from Fgfr2-IIIc to Fgfr2-IIIb.
source: Conversely, ectopic expression of Esrp1 in mesenchymal cells induces a switch from Fgfr2-IIIc to Fgfr2-IIIb, indicating that the ESRPs are necessary and sufficient to enforce expression of the epithelial Fgfr2-IIIb isoform (Warzecha et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from previous work by the authors.

claim: The ESRPs are necessary and sufficient to enforce expression of the epithelial Fgfr2-IIIb isoform.
source: Conversely, ectopic expression of Esrp1 in mesenchymal cells induces a switch from Fgfr2-IIIc to Fgfr2-IIIb, indicating that the ESRPs are necessary and sufficient to enforce expression of the epithelial Fgfr2-IIIb isoform (Warzecha et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that Esrp1 expression can induce the switch.

claim: ESRP targets are enriched for genes involved in epithelial cell properties such as cytoskeletal dynamics, cell motility, cell–cell junctions, and pathways involved in EMT.
source: Importantly, ESRP targets are enriched for genes involved in epithelial cell properties such as cytoskeletal dynamics, cell motility, cell–cell junctions, and pathways involved in EMT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from previous cell culture studies by the authors.

claim: Esrp1 and Esrp2 are specifically expressed in epithelial cells in numerous organs in adult mice.
source: The ESRP mouse homologues, Esrp1 and Esrp2, are specifically expressed in epithelial cells in numerous organs in adult mice and are essentially absent in mesenchymal cells and other non-epithelial cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including in situ hybridization and microarray analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Esrp1 and Esrp2 are essentially absent in mesenchymal cells and other non-epithelial cell types.
source: The ESRP mouse homologues, Esrp1 and Esrp2, are specifically expressed in epithelial cells in numerous organs in adult mice and are essentially absent in mesenchymal cells and other non-epithelial cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including in situ hybridization and microarray analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Esrp2 null mice are viable and fertile.
source: Whereas Esrp2 null mice are viable and fertile, we demonstrate that KO of Esrp1 alone is neonatal lethal at Postnatal Day (P) 0, associated with fully penetrant bilateral cleft lip and palate (CL/P).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the Esrp2 knockout mice generated in the study.

claim: KO of Esrp1 alone is neonatal lethal at Postnatal Day (P) 0.
source: Whereas Esrp2 null mice are viable and fertile, we demonstrate that KO of Esrp1 alone is neonatal lethal at Postnatal Day (P) 0, associated with fully penetrant bilateral cleft lip and palate (CL/P).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the Esrp1 knockout mice generated in the study.

claim: KO of Esrp1 is associated with fully penetrant bilateral cleft lip and palate (CL/P).
source: Whereas Esrp2 null mice are viable and fertile, we demonstrate that KO of Esrp1 alone is neonatal lethal at Postnatal Day (P) 0, associated with fully penetrant bilateral cleft lip and palate (CL/P).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the Esrp1 knockout mice showing 100% penetrance of the phenotype.

claim: Esrp1 KO combined with loss of Esrp2 resulted in more pronounced defects in organogenesis.
source: Esrp1 KO combined with loss of Esrp2 resulted in more pronounced defects in organogenesis that will be described herein.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from double knockout mice showing more severe phenotypes than Esrp1 KO alone.

claim: Excision of exons 7–9 following Cre-mediated recombination removes the first RNA Recognition Motif (RRM), and places the remaining transcript out of frame, generating a null allele of Esrp1.
source: Excision of exons 7–9 following Cre-mediated recombination removes the first RNA Recognition Motif (RRM), and places the remaining transcript out of frame, generating a null allele of Esrp1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and validation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mice with germline KO of Esrp1 exhibited fully penetrant bilateral cleft lip and cleft palate (CL/P).
source: In contrast, mice with germline KO of Esrp1 exhibited fully penetrant bilateral cleft lip and cleft palate (CL/P), and these mice are neonatal lethal on post natal day 0 (P0) most likely due to orofacial clefting.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from all Esrp1 KO mice examined (n > 40 embryos).

claim: Esrp1 KO mice are neonatal lethal on post natal day 0 (P0) most likely due to orofacial clefting.
source: In contrast, mice with germline KO of Esrp1 exhibited fully penetrant bilateral cleft lip and cleft palate (CL/P), and these mice are neonatal lethal on post natal day 0 (P0) most likely due to orofacial clefting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that all Esrp1 KO mice die at P0 and have cleft lip/palate.

claim: Esrp1 is necessary for craniofacial development and post-natal viability.
source: Therefore, while Esrp2 is not essential in mice with intact Esrp1 alleles, Esrp1 is necessary for craniofacial development and post-natal viability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing neonatal lethality and craniofacial defects in Esrp1 KO mice.

claim: KO embryos were normal in size.
source: Overall embryo metrics including weight and crown to rump length showed KO embryos were normal in size, KH embryos were only slightly reduced in weight and length compared to WT littermate embryos, whereas DKO embryos showed a ∼30% reduction in length (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E.

claim: KH embryos were only slightly reduced in weight and length compared to WT littermate embryos.
source: Overall embryo metrics including weight and crown to rump length showed KO embryos were normal in size, KH embryos were only slightly reduced in weight and length compared to WT littermate embryos, whereas DKO embryos showed a ∼30% reduction in length (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E.

claim: DKO embryos showed a ∼30% reduction in length.
source: Overall embryo metrics including weight and crown to rump length showed KO embryos were normal in size, KH embryos were only slightly reduced in weight and length compared to WT littermate embryos, whereas DKO embryos showed a ∼30% reduction in length (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E.

claim: Esrp1 KO embryos exhibited bilateral cleft lip and clefting of the primary and secondary hard palate, as well as the soft palate.
source: Esrp1 KO embryos exhibited bilateral cleft lip and clefting of the primary and secondary hard palate, as well as the soft palate (n > 40 embryos evaluated).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from gross morphological analysis of E18.5 embryos.

claim: KH and DKO embryos exhibited more pronounced craniofacial defects including profound rostral shortening, and mandibular hypoplasia and dysplasia.
source: This phenotype was also observed in KH and DKO embryos, but these embryos also exhibited more pronounced craniofacial defects including profound rostral shortening, and mandibular hypoplasia and dysplasia (Figure 1A–L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from gross morphological analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: DKO mice presented with the most severe defects, resulting in a malformed mandible lacking the normal curvature seen in control embryos.
source: DKO mice presented with the most severe defects, resulting in a malformed mandible lacking the normal curvature seen in control embryos (Figure 1M–P,U–X).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from bone and cartilage staining shown in Figure 1.

claim: The mandibles of Esrp KO embryos lacked the coronoid process.
source: The mandibles of Esrp KO embryos lacked the coronoid process (Figure 1U–X), which explains the widened oral opening in the Esrp deficient mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from bone and cartilage staining shown in Figure 1.

claim: The lack of coronoid process explains the widened oral opening in the Esrp deficient mice.
source: The mandibles of Esrp KO embryos lacked the coronoid process (Figure 1U–X), which explains the widened oral opening in the Esrp deficient mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical observation of missing coronoid process.

claim: Esrp2 can partially compensate for loss of Esrp1, as craniofacial phenotypes observed in Esrp1 KO mice are more profound in combination with deletion of one or both alleles of Esrp2.
source: These studies also demonstrate that Esrp2 can partially compensate for loss of Esrp1, as craniofacial phenotypes observed in Esrp1 KO mice are more profound in combination with deletion of one or both alleles of Esrp2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing progressively more severe phenotypes with loss of Esrp2 alleles.

claim: Esrp KH embryos often presented with malformed forelimbs and forepaw syndactyly.
source: Whereas we observed no gross forelimb or hindlimb defects in Esrp1 KO mice, Esrp KH embryos often presented with malformed forelimbs and forepaw syndactyly (n = 22 evaluated).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from examination of E18.5 embryos.

claim: In DKO E18.5 embryos the forelimbs were further malformed, associated with smaller limbs and full fusion of the forepaw, or partially penetrant forelimb agenesis (∼33%, n = 9/27 evaluated).
source: In DKO E18.5 embryos the forelimbs were further malformed, associated with smaller limbs and full fusion of the forepaw, or partially penetrant forelimb agenesis (∼33%, n = 9/27 evaluated).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from examination of E18.5 embryos.

claim: The forelimb defect was associated with the absence of the radius and humerus bones.
source: Bone and cartilage stains revealed the forelimb defect was associated with the absence of the radius and humerus bones (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from bone and cartilage staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Hindlimbs were unaffected in Esrp KO mice.
source: However, hindlimbs were unaffected in Esrp KO mice and therefore the molecular cues driving formation of forelimb and hindlimbs clearly differ with respect to a requirement for Esrp regulated splicing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from examination of E18.5 embryos.

claim: The molecular cues driving formation of forelimb and hindlimbs clearly differ with respect to a requirement for Esrp regulated splicing.
source: However, hindlimbs were unaffected in Esrp KO mice and therefore the molecular cues driving formation of forelimb and hindlimbs clearly differ with respect to a requirement for Esrp regulated splicing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that forelimbs are affected but hindlimbs are not in Esrp KO mice.

claim: Fgfr2-IIIb KO mice exhibit CPO and absence of both forelimbs and hindlimbs.
source: This is most evident in the craniofacial and limb defects, where KO of Esrp1 alone results in bilateral cleft lip and palate and DKO embryos have forelimb defects, whereas Fgfr2-IIIb KO mice exhibit CPO and absence of both forelimbs and hindlimbs (De Moerlooze et al., 2000; Rice et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: We observed agenesis of two organs that undergo branching morphogenesis, lung and salivary gland, in the DKO embryos.
source: We observed agenesis of two organs that undergo branching morphogenesis, lung and salivary gland, in the DKO embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Kidneys are present in the KO and DKO embryos, albeit reduced in size.
source: Kidneys, which undergo a stereotypical branching morphogenesis, are present in the KO and DKO embryos, albeit reduced in size.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The epithelial cells that comprise the skin exhibit high levels of Esrp1 and Esrp2, both in the interfollicular epidermis as well as the epithelial cells of the hair follicle.
source: Previous studies have shown that the epithelial cells that comprise the skin exhibit high levels of Esrp1 and Esrp2, both in the interfollicular epidermis as well as the epithelial cells of the hair follicle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,E) (Su et al., 2002; Rendl et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2008; Greco et al., 2009; Warzecha et al., 2009a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: DKO embryos had thin transparent skin at E18.5.
source: However, DKO embryos had thin transparent skin at E18.5.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation of DKO embryos.

claim: Histological analysis of DKO and control littermates revealed epidermal hypoplasia.
source: Histological analysis of DKO and control littermates revealed epidermal hypoplasia (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from histological analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Quantification of epidermal thickness in DKO skin was reduced by 35% compared to littermate controls.
source: Quantification of epidermal thickness, as measured from the basal keratinocyte layer to the granular layer, in DKO skin was reduced by 35% compared to littermate controls carrying at least one wild type copy of Esrp1 (Control: 25.79 ± 2.20 μm, n = 8, DKO: 16.68 ± 1.66 μm, n = 6, unpaired two-tailed t test p < 0.0001) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In DKO skin there were ∼23% fewer hair follicles.
source: In DKO skin there were ∼23% fewer hair follicles (Control: 16.00 ± 2.37, n = 8, DKO: 12.25 ± 1.24, n = 6, unpaired two-tailed t test p = 0.0043) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The reduced number of hair follicles in DKO skin was associated with earlier staged hair follicles compared to controls, indicating delayed hair follicle maturation.
source: Moreover, the reduced number of hair follicles in DKO skin was associated with earlier staged hair follicles compared to controls, indicating delayed hair follicle maturation (Figure 2D) (Paus et al., 1999; Petiot et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and citations to published literature on hair follicle staging.

claim: DKO skin sections stained positively for epidermal differentiation markers.
source: DKO skin sections stained positively for these differentiation markers; however, Keratin 14, Keratin 10, Loricrin, and Filaggrin expression domains were reduced in overall size compared to the control skin samples (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Keratin 14, Keratin 10, Loricrin, and Filaggrin expression domains were reduced in overall size in DKO skin compared to the control skin samples.
source: DKO skin sections stained positively for these differentiation markers; however, Keratin 14, Keratin 10, Loricrin, and Filaggrin expression domains were reduced in overall size compared to the control skin samples (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: DKO epidermis is still capable of forming a stratified epidermis.
source: This is consistent with the observed epidermal hypoplasia, and illustrates that DKO epidermis nonetheless is still capable of forming a stratified epidermis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that all epidermal layers are present despite being thinner.

claim: Hair formation was functionally intact in DKO skin, although overall follicle number was reduced.
source: Thus, hair formation was also functionally intact, although overall follicle number was reduced in DKO skin.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that hair follicles present in DKO skin show appropriate markers of hair formation.

claim: These skin phenotypes are similar to those previously observed in Fgfr2-IIIb isoform-specific KO mice that also showed epidermal hypoplasia and reduced and immature hair follicle numbers.
source: These skin phenotypes are similar to those previously observed in Fgfr2-IIIb isoform-specific KO mice that also showed epidermal hypoplasia and reduced and immature hair follicle numbers (Petiot et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: No change in Fgfr2-IIIb (epithelial) splicing was detected until both Esrp1 and Esrp2 were deleted.
source: Across all nine allelic combinations no change in Fgfr2-IIIb (epithelial) splicing was detected until both Esrp1 and Esrp2 were deleted, and thus only a single copy of Esrp2 is sufficient to maintain Fgfr2-IIIb splicing in epidermis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis of Fgfr2 splicing.

claim: Only a single copy of Esrp2 is sufficient to maintain Fgfr2-IIIb splicing in epidermis.
source: Across all nine allelic combinations no change in Fgfr2-IIIb (epithelial) splicing was detected until both Esrp1 and Esrp2 were deleted, and thus only a single copy of Esrp2 is sufficient to maintain Fgfr2-IIIb splicing in epidermis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing no change in Fgfr2 splicing until both Esrps are deleted.

claim: In DKO epidermis Fgfr2 underwent a full switch from Fgfr2-IIIb (epithelial) to Fgfr2-IIIc (mesenchymal).
source: However, in DKO epidermis Fgfr2 underwent a full switch from Fgfr2-IIIb (epithelial) to Fgfr2-IIIc (mesenchymal), indicating that the production of the Fgfr2-IIIb isoform is fully dependent upon the Esrps in epidermis (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The production of the Fgfr2-IIIb isoform is fully dependent upon the Esrps in epidermis.
source: However, in DKO epidermis Fgfr2 underwent a full switch from Fgfr2-IIIb (epithelial) to Fgfr2-IIIc (mesenchymal), indicating that the production of the Fgfr2-IIIb isoform is fully dependent upon the Esrps in epidermis (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing complete switch in Fgfr2 splicing in DKO epidermis.

claim: In both Fgfr1 and Fgfr3, we observed a complete switch from exon IIIb to exon IIIc splicing in DKO epidermis.
source: In both Fgfr1 and Fgfr3, we also observed a complete switch from exon IIIb to exon IIIc splicing in DKO epidermis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Fgfr1 showed a more dramatic switch in splicing in Esrp1 KO epidermis than Fgfr3.
source: However, Fgfr1 showed a more dramatic switch in splicing in Esrp1 KO epidermis than Fgfr3, but both showed a gradual switch to the -IIIc isoforms upon sequential loss of the Esrps (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Esrps are central in the regulation of the Fgfr family of tyrosine kinase receptors.
source: This places the Esrps central in the regulation of this developmentally significant family of tyrosine kinase receptors, where loss of both Esrp1 and Esrp2 results in a splicing switch to the mesenchymal receptor isoforms in the epidermis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing Esrp regulation of Fgfr1, Fgfr2, and Fgfr3 splicing.

claim: Loss of both Esrp1 and Esrp2 results in a splicing switch to the mesenchymal receptor isoforms in the epidermis.
source: This places the Esrps central in the regulation of this developmentally significant family of tyrosine kinase receptors, where loss of both Esrp1 and Esrp2 results in a splicing switch to the mesenchymal receptor isoforms in the epidermis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis of Fgfr splicing.

claim: Enah is more profoundly affected by loss of Esrp1.
source: Enah is more profoundly affected by loss of Esrp1, while Arhgef11 remains relatively unchanged until the KH and DKO samples (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Arhgef11 remains relatively unchanged until the KH and DKO samples.
source: Enah is more profoundly affected by loss of Esrp1, while Arhgef11 remains relatively unchanged until the KH and DKO samples (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Esrp regulated splicing events show differential sensitivity to loss of Esrp1 and Esrp2.
source: These results indicate differential sensitivity of Esrp regulated splicing events to loss of Esrp1 and Esrp2, and thus variable functional redundancy of Esrp1 and Esrp2 in regulation of Esrp-mediated splicing events.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing different splicing patterns across different genetic combinations.

claim: There is variable functional redundancy of Esrp1 and Esrp2 in regulation of Esrp-mediated splicing events.
source: These results indicate differential sensitivity of Esrp regulated splicing events to loss of Esrp1 and Esrp2, and thus variable functional redundancy of Esrp1 and Esrp2 in regulation of Esrp-mediated splicing events.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing different degrees of compensation by Esrp2 for different targets.

claim: The largest number and greatest ΔPSI in detected splicing switches were seen in the DKO epidermis.
source: As expected, the largest number and greatest ΔPSI in detected splicing switches were seen in the DKO epidermis (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The majority of AS events were identified in the SE category and comprise 55–72% of the total detected Esrp-dependent AS.
source: The majority of AS events were identified in the SE category and comprise 55–72% of the total detected Esrp-dependent AS (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Fgfr1, Fgfr2, and Fgfr3 were found within the top statistically significant events for the MXE category from the WT vs DKO comparison.
source: For example, Fgfr1, Fgfr2, and Fgfr3 were found within the top statistically significant events for the MXE category from the WT vs DKO comparison.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The Esrps are primary regulators of the CD44v isoform, where ESRP depletion led to a nearly complete switch towards the mesenchymal CD44s isoform in human cell lines.
source: The Esrps were shown to be primary regulators of the CD44v isoform, where ESRP depletion led to a nearly complete switch towards the mesenchymal CD44s isoform in human cell lines (Warzecha et al., 2009a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The predicted ΔPSI as measured by rMATS and the ΔPSI determined by semi quantitative RT-PCR showed a high correlation (r-value = 0.98, p < 0.0001).
source: Comparison of the predicted ΔPSI as measured by rMATS and the ΔPSI determined by semi quantitative RT-PCR revealed a high correlation between these two measurements in WT and DKO samples (r-value = 0.98, p < 0.0001, Pearson Correlation) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing RNA-seq and RT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The inclusion of exon 5 in Grhl1 maintains Grhl1 expression, whereas skipping results in a transcript targeted by NMD.
source: The inclusion of exon 5 maintains Grhl1 expression, whereas skipping as seen in the DKO epidermis results in a transcript targeted by NMD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that exon 5 skipping introduces a premature termination codon.

claim: In DKO epidermis there is an 85% reduction in exon 5 inclusion that results in an 86% reduction in Grhl1 transcript levels.
source: In DKO epidermis there is an 85% reduction in exon 5 inclusion that results in an 86% reduction in Grhl1 transcript levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B, see also Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR and qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: Esrp regulated splicing targets were enriched for the functional GO terms 'cytoskeletal protein binding', 'cell cortex', 'vesicle-mediated transport', and 'actin binding'.
source: Esrp regulated splicing targets were enriched for the functional GO terms 'cytoskeletal protein binding', 'cell cortex', 'vesicle-mediated transport', and 'actin binding' as well as the KEGG pathway terms 'adhererns junction' and 'MAPK signaling pathway' (FDR [Benjamini-Hochberg] <0.05).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq data using DAVID 6.7.

claim: Esrp regulated splicing targets were enriched for the KEGG pathway terms 'adhererns junction' and 'MAPK signaling pathway'.
source: Esrp regulated splicing targets were enriched for the functional GO terms 'cytoskeletal protein binding', 'cell cortex', 'vesicle-mediated transport', and 'actin binding' as well as the KEGG pathway terms 'adhererns junction' and 'MAPK signaling pathway' (FDR [Benjamini-Hochberg] <0.05).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of RNA-seq data using DAVID 6.7.

claim: The enrichment of these biological processes and pathways support an important functional role of the Esrps in regulated splicing of genes in pathways necessary for proper epithelial cell maintenance and function.
source: The enrichment of these biological processes and pathways support an important functional role of the Esrps in regulated splicing of genes in pathways necessary for proper epithelial cell maintenance and function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene ontology and pathway analysis results.

claim: There were some modest changes in expression of candidate splicing factors with statistically significant changes in expression following Esrp ablation.
source: We noted large changes in Esrp1 and Esrp2 expression in DKO epidermis, but there were some more modest changes in expression of other candidate splicing factors with statistically significant changes in expression following Esrp ablation (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A loss of Esrp expression is likely to play a major role in splicing of numerous transcripts.
source: Hence, while a loss of Esrp expression is likely to play a major role in splicing of numerous transcripts, alterations in expression of some of these other candidate regulators may also contribute to splicing shifts in some targets.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Esrp expression changes are the largest, but other splicing factors also change.

claim: Alterations in expression of some other candidate regulators may also contribute to splicing shifts in some targets.
source: Hence, while a loss of Esrp expression is likely to play a major role in splicing of numerous transcripts, alterations in expression of some of these other candidate regulators may also contribute to splicing shifts in some targets.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that other splicing factors show expression changes.

claim: The top ranked Esrp1 (UGGUGG) binding site motif was identified in the upstream intron of Esrp silenced SE events in all three pairwise comparisons.
source: Motif enrichment analysis of known splicing factor binding sites identified the top ranked Esrp1 (UGGUGG) binding site motif defined by SELEX in the upstream intron of Esrp silenced SE events in all three pairwise comparisons, and the Esrp1 motif was also enriched in the exon body of Esrp1 KO splicing targets (Dittmar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The Esrp1 motif was enriched in the exon body of Esrp1 KO splicing targets.
source: Motif enrichment analysis of known splicing factor binding sites identified the top ranked Esrp1 (UGGUGG) binding site motif defined by SELEX in the upstream intron of Esrp silenced SE events in all three pairwise comparisons, and the Esrp1 motif was also enriched in the exon body of Esrp1 KO splicing targets (Dittmar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Enrichment of the Esrp1 motif was observed in the downstream intron of Esrp enhanced exons in the KO and DKO analysis.
source: We also observed enrichment of the Esrp1 motif in the downstream intron of Esrp enhanced exons in the KO and DKO analysis.
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: This is consistent with the Esrp RNA binding map identified from in vitro Esrp targets, wherein Esrp binding in the upstream intron or in the exon body of a regulated SE events mediates exon skipping, and conversely binding in the downstream intron promotes exon inclusion.
source: This is consistent with the Esrp RNA binding map identified from our in vitro Esrp targets, wherein Esrp binding in the upstream intron or in the exon body of a regulated SE events mediates exon skipping, and conversely binding in the downstream intron promotes exon inclusion (Dittmar et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The enrichment of Esrp motifs and their positional enrichment relative to the regulated exons suggest that many or most of the identified splicing events are likely direct targets.
source: However, the differential expression of the Esrps together with the enrichment of Esrp binding motifs and their positional enrichment relative to the regulated exons further suggest that many or most of the identified splicing events are likely direct targets.
evidence: This is an inference based on the motif enrichment analysis and known mechanisms of splicing regulation.

claim: We identified 572 significant changes in gene expression, with >twofold difference in gene expression and FDR < 5% based on average FPKM in at least one pairwise comparison of the four genetic groupings.
source: We identified 572 significant changes in gene expression, with >twofold difference in gene expression and FDR < 5% based on average FPKM in at least one pairwise comparison of the four genetic groupings (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The most predominant changes in expression are observed between WT and DKO embryonic epidermis.
source: The differential gene expression analysis revealed that by far the most predominant changes in expression are observed between WT and DKO embryonic epidermis.
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: In the WT vs DKO group there were 514 significant changes in gene expression, of which 65% (337/514) were down regulated and 35% (178/514) were up regulated in the DKO epidermis.
source: In the WT vs DKO group there were 514 significant changes in gene expression, of which 65% (337/514) were down regulated and 35% (178/514) were up regulated in the DKO epidermis.
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The DEGs were enriched for the GO terms 'epidermal cell differentiation', 'keratinocyte differentiation', 'oxidation reduction', and 'fatty acid metabolic process'.
source: The DEGs were enriched for the GO terms 'epidermal cell differentiation', 'keratinocyte differentiation', 'oxidation reduction', and 'fatty acid metabolic process' (FDR [Benjamini-Hochberg] <0.05) (Figure 6B, Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis of differentially expressed genes shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In the DKO epidermis we saw up regulation of several EDC genes, including the Sprr (1a, 1b, 2b, 2d, 2e, 2g, 2h), Lce (3b, 3c, 3f), S100 (a4, a6, a9), and Repetin (Rptn) and Cornelin (Crnn) genes.
source: In the DKO epidermis we saw up regulation of several EDC genes, including the Sprr (1a, 1b, 2b, 2d, 2e, 2g, 2h), Lce (3b, 3c, 3f), S100 (a4, a6, a9), and Repetin (Rptn) and Cornelin (Crnn) genes.
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: We observed up regulation of epidermal differentiation associated genes including numerous Keratins (2, 6a, 6b, 12, 13, 16, 23, 34, 84).
source: We also observed up regulation of epidermal differentiation associated genes including numerous Keratins (2, 6a, 6b, 12, 13, 16, 23, 34, 84).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Up regulation of EDC genes is often associated with mouse models harboring skin barrier defects.
source: Up regulation of EDC genes as well as changes in other genes are often associated with mouse models harboring skin barrier defects, such as Loricrin, Klf4, and Grhl3 KO mouse models (Segre et al., 1999; Koch et al., 2000; Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The up regulation of EDC gene expression is believed to be a compensatory response to stress or breakdown of the skin barrier function.
source: While the mechanism of up regulating EDC gene expression is not well understood, it is believed to be a compensatory response to stress or breakdown of the skin barrier function.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about EDC gene regulation in barrier defects.

claim: These changes in EDC genes and Keratins are mostly an indirect effect of the Esrp KO.
source: Because very similar changes in gene expression are observed in Esrp1/Esrp2 DKO epidermis as those in other mouse KO models associated with barrier defects, we believe these changes in EDC genes and Keratins are mostly an indirect effect of the Esrp KO, in contrast to the direct regulation of Grhl1 by AS-NMD.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with other mouse models and the mechanism of Grhl1 regulation.

claim: These collective changes in gene expression suggest epithelial barrier dysfunction in the epidermis associated with the loss of the Esrps.
source: These collective changes in gene expression suggest epithelial barrier dysfunction in the epidermis associated with the loss of the Esrps.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression changes observed in DKO epidermis.

claim: Krt14-DKO neonates were viable at birth (P0.5).
source: Krt14-DKO neonates were viable at birth (P0.5), however no Krt14-DKO pups with confirmed Esrp1 KO survived to the following day (P1.5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation of conditional knockout mice.

claim: No Krt14-DKO pups with confirmed Esrp1 KO survived to the following day (P1.5).
source: Krt14-DKO neonates were viable at birth (P0.5), however no Krt14-DKO pups with confirmed Esrp1 KO survived to the following day (P1.5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation of conditional knockout mice.

claim: Control littermates lost weight at expected levels, but never exceeded ∼1.5% of total body weight, indicative of an intact epidermal barrier.
source: During the time-course control littermates lost weight at expected levels, but never exceeded ∼1.5% of total body weight, indicative of an intact epidermal barrier.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the water loss assay.

claim: Krt14-DKO pups lost significantly more weight (∼2.5–3% of total body weight) compared to littermate controls during the same time period.
source: However, Krt14-DKO pups lost significantly more weight (∼2.5–3% of total body weight) compared to littermate controls during the same time period (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the water loss assay shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The Krt14-Cre DKO mice that exhibited weight loss during the water loss assay also displayed skin phenotypes observed in other mouse KO models associated with skin barrier defects: thin red shinny skin with areas of dry flaky skin.
source: The Krt14-Cre DKO mice that exhibited weight loss during the water loss assay also displayed skin phenotypes observed in other mouse KO models associated with skin barrier defects: thin red shinny skin with areas of dry flaky skin (Figure 7A) (Koch et al., 2000; Gladden et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation and citations to published literature.

claim: The Krt14-DKO mice share the differential expression of EDC and Keratin genes, consistent with the observed skin barrier defect.
source: Therefore, the Krt14-DKO mice share the differential expression of EDC and Keratin genes, consistent with the observed skin barrier defect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the qRT-PCR validation of gene expression changes in Krt14-DKO epidermis.

claim: These observations implicate the Esrps in the regulation of skin barrier function, a fundamental characteristic of epithelial cells in the epidermis.
source: Taken together these observations implicate the Esrps in the regulation of skin barrier function, a fundamental characteristic of epithelial cells in the epidermis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing barrier defects in conditional knockout mice.

claim: The Esrp-directed splicing network generates epithelial specific or enriched protein isoforms that are likely to be required for epithelial cell barrier function in epithelial cells throughout mammalian organisms.
source: Therefore, the Esrp-directed splicing network generates epithelial specific or enriched protein isoforms that are likely to be required for epithelial cell barrier function in epithelial cells throughout mammalian organisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that barrier function is a fundamental property of epithelia in many organs.

claim: The numerous developmental defects identified in Esrp KO mice demonstrate an essential role for Esrp-regulated splicing in the development of many organ systems.
source: The numerous developmental defects we identified in these mice demonstrate an essential role for Esrp-regulated splicing in the development of many organ systems.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the multiple organ defects observed in Esrp knockout mice.

claim: Loss of both Esrp1 and Esrp2 manifests the most severe phenotypes.
source: Using germline KOs for Esrp1 and Esrp2 we demonstrate a requirement for Esrp1 during embryonic development and postnatal survival, with loss of both proteins manifesting the most severe phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing progressively more severe phenotypes in double knockout mice.

claim: Global changes in gene expression accompanying loss of the Esrps in the skin of the germline DKO mice revealed an epidermal barrier defect.
source: Global changes in gene expression accompanying loss of the Esrps in the skin of the germline DKO mice revealed an epidermal barrier defect that was confirmed using conditional ablation of the Esrps in the epithelial cells that constitute the epidermis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq and water loss assay.

claim: The epidermal barrier defect was confirmed using conditional ablation of the Esrps in the epithelial cells that constitute the epidermis.
source: Global changes in gene expression accompanying loss of the Esrps in the skin of the germline DKO mice revealed an epidermal barrier defect that was confirmed using conditional ablation of the Esrps in the epithelial cells that constitute the epidermis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from conditional knockout mice showing barrier defects.

claim: These observations provide strong evidence for the cell autonomous requirement of the Esrps in epidermal development and programs of epithelial-specific splicing in organogenesis and epithelial cell function.
source: Together, these observations provide strong evidence for the cell autonomous requirement of the Esrps in epidermal development and programs of epithelial-specific splicing in organogenesis and epithelial cell function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that conditional knockout in epidermis recapitulates the barrier defect.

claim: The Esrp KO mouse is a unique model for CL/P.
source: Therefore, the Esrp KO mouse is a unique model that can be used to further evaluate the role of epithelial-specific splicing regulation in lip and palate formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that there are few mouse models for CL/P and the Esrp KO shows this phenotype.

claim: The functional redundancy of the Esrps during development is consistent with in vitro observations at the level of AS.
source: The functional redundancy of the Esrps during development is consistent with our in vitro observations at the level of AS.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of in vivo and in vitro data.

claim: The progression of phenotypes could be due to the degree of change in AS mediated by loss of Esrp1 alone or in combination with Esrp2.
source: Therefore, the progression of phenotypes could be due to the degree of change in AS mediated by loss of Esrp1 alone or in combination with Esrp2.
evidence: This is speculation based on the correlation between splicing changes and phenotype severity.

claim: Esrp DKO embryos do not fully phenocopy the defects previously seen in Fgfr2-IIIb KO mice.
source: It is of note that despite the fact that the Esrps are required for expression of Fgfr2-IIIb, Esrp DKO embryos do not fully phenocopy the defects previously seen in Fgfr2-IIIb KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of phenotypes between Esrp DKO and Fgfr2-IIIb KO mice.

claim: Part of the discrepancy between Esrp DKO and Fgfr2-IIIb KO phenotypes can be accounted for by differences in the manner in which Fgfr2 splicing is altered in each model.
source: Part of this discrepancy can likely be accounted for by differences in the manner in which Fgfr2 splicing is altered in each model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different molecular outcomes of the two knockout strategies.

claim: In Esrp DKO mice, there is a switch in splicing from exon IIIb to IIIc that would still encode a functional receptor, albeit one with altered ligand binding specificities.
source: In our mice, there is a switch in splicing from exon IIIb to IIIc in Esrp DKO mice that would still encode a functional receptor, albeit one with altered ligand binding specificities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of the Fgfr2-IIIc isoform.

claim: The deletion of exon IIIb in Fgfr2-IIIb KO mice does not result in default splicing to exon IIIc in epithelial cells, but instead results primarily in skipping of both exons IIIb and IIIc.
source: In contrast, the deletion of exon IIIb in Fgfr2-IIIb KO mice does not result in default splicing to exon IIIc in epithelial cells, but instead results primarily in skipping of both exons IIIb and IIIc, thereby inactivating Fgfr2 expression altogether in epithelial cells, but retaining Fgfr2-IIIc in mesenchymal cells.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the Fgfr2-IIIb KO model from published literature.

claim: In some contexts, autocrine or paracrine functions of Fgf ligands for Fgfr2-IIIc may compensate for the switch in Fgfr2 splicing.
source: Hence in some contexts, autocrine or paracrine functions of Fgf ligands for Fgfr2-IIIc may compensate for the switch in Fgfr2 splicing, but not in others.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms that could explain phenotypic differences.

claim: Esrp ablation induces global changes in AS that contribute to the phenotypes observed.
source: However, it must also be emphasized that Esrp ablation also induces global changes in AS that surely contribute to the phenotypes we observe, including those, such as cleft lip, that were not identified in Fgfr2-IIIb KO mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data showing many splicing changes beyond Fgfr2.

claim: Alterations in Fgf receptor splicing and Fgf signaling contribute to the phenotypes observed in the epidermis.
source: In the epidermis, we suspect that alterations in Fgf receptor splicing and Fgf signaling contribute to the phenotypes we observed since epidermal hypoplasia was observed in both Fgfr2-IIIb and Esrp1/Esrp2 DKO skin.
evidence: This is speculation based on the similarity of phenotypes between Fgfr2-IIIb KO and Esrp DKO.

claim: Conditional KO of Fgfr2-IIIb in the epidermis is not lethal.
source: However, conditional KO of Fgfr2-IIIb as well as combined KO of Fgfr2 and Fgfr1-IIIb in the epidermis is not lethal unlike the post-natal lethality we observe when Esrp1 and Esrp2 are conditionally ablated in epidermis.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from published literature about conditional Fgfr KO models.

claim: Splicing changes in additional Esrp target transcripts are required for the lethal barrier defect observed in conditional Esrp KO.
source: These observations, combined with the fact that Esrp1/Esrp2 ablation in the epidermis is associated with an isoform switch rather than complete loss of function of Fgfr1 and Fgfr2 receptor proteins, strongly suggest that splicing changes in additional Esrp target transcripts are required for the lethal barrier defect we observe.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of phenotypes between Fgfr KO and Esrp KO models.

claim: The challenge for future studies will be to identify the individual or combined splicing events that underlie the observed phenotypes in the skin as well as other tissues and organs.
source: Therefore, the challenge for future studies will be to identify the individual or combined splicing events that underlie the observed phenotypes in the skin as well as other tissues and organs.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.

claim: In many of the Esrp targets we identified large 'switch-like' changes in AS with the loss of the Esrps.
source: In many of the Esrp targets we identified large 'switch-like' changes in AS with the loss of the Esrps.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq and RT-PCR analysis.

claim: These changes in AS would lead to an altered proteomic landscape by the loss or introduction of different protein isoforms.
source: These changes would lead to an altered proteomic landscape by the loss or introduction of different protein isoforms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known relationship between alternative splicing and protein isoforms.

claim: These changes in protein isoforms likely underlie the observed phenotypes in the Esrp deficient mice.
source: These changes in protein isoforms likely underlie the observed phenotypes in the Esrp deficient mice.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the phenotypes.

claim: The differential sensitivity of AS events partly reflects reduced splicing activity of Esrp2 compared to Esrp1.
source: The fact that Esrp2 can only partially compensate for loss of Esrp1 in the epidermis, despite retaining high expression in Esrp1 KO mice, indicates that this differential sensitivity partly reflects reduced splicing activity of Esrp2 compared to Esrp1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Esrp2 cannot fully compensate for Esrp1 loss despite high expression.

claim: The levels of both Esrp1 and Esrp2 expression are high in the epidermis (Average FPKM: Esrp1 130, Esrp2 127).
source: It is important to emphasize that the levels of both Esrp1 and Esrp2 expression are high in the epidermis (Average FPKM: Esrp1 130, Esrp2 127), which in turn could impart greater functional redundancy in the epidermis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: High expression of both Esrp1 and Esrp2 in the epidermis could impart greater functional redundancy.
source: It is important to emphasize that the levels of both Esrp1 and Esrp2 expression are high in the epidermis (Average FPKM: Esrp1 130, Esrp2 127), which in turn could impart greater functional redundancy in the epidermis.
evidence: This is speculation about the relationship between expression levels and functional redundancy.

claim: Most epithelial cells express less Esrp2 relative to Esrp1.
source: However, not all epithelial cells express Esrp1 or Esrp2 as highly as in the skin and most epithelial cells express less Esrp2 relative to Esrp1 (Su et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The differences in phenotypes observed in the Esrp1 KO and Esrp1/Esrp2 DKO may reflect splicing alteration in specific transcripts for which Esrp2 cannot fully compensate for loss of Esrp1 and/or be reflective of differences in Esrp2 levels in different epithelia.
source: The differences in phenotypes observed in the Esrp1 KO and Esrp1/Esrp2 DKO may therefore reflect splicing alteration in specific transcripts for which Esrp2 cannot fully compensate for loss of Esrp1 and/or be reflective of differences in Esrp2 levels in different epithelia.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms underlying phenotypic differences.

claim: The SE events identified from the KO epidermis were enriched for Esrp binding motifs in the upstream intron and exon body of silenced exons, and within the downstream intron of enhanced exons proximal to the 5′ splice site.
source: The SE events identified from the KO epidermis were enriched for Esrp binding motifs in the upstream intron and exon body of silenced exons, and within the downstream intron of enhanced exons proximal to the 5′ splice site.
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: This RNA binding map is consistent with strong repression and enhancement, respectively.
source: This RNA binding map is consistent with strong repression and enhancement, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on known mechanisms of splicing regulation by position-dependent binding.

claim: This motif enrichment pattern is most strikingly observed in the KO dataset, as the exon body enrichment is reduced/lost in the KH and DKO samples.
source: This motif enrichment pattern is most strikingly observed in the KO dataset, as the exon body enrichment is reduced/lost in the KH and DKO samples.
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis comparing different genetic groups.

claim: The Esrp1 KO sensitive AS events require more Esrp binding sites for maintenance of the Esrp-directed splicing pattern.
source: This describes a potential mechanism in which the Esrp1 KO sensitive AS events require more Esrp binding sites for maintenance of the Esrp-directed splicing pattern.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying differential sensitivity based on motif enrichment patterns.

claim: In the absence of Esrp1 expression, Esrp2 is not sufficient to drive AS regulation or to block the activity of other splicing factors that promote the opposite pattern of splicing.
source: In the absence of Esrp1 expression, Esrp2 is not sufficient to drive AS regulation or to block the activity of other splicing factors that promote the opposite pattern of splicing.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of Esrp2 compensation based on the motif enrichment data.

claim: It is likely that other splicing factors contribute to the regulation of Esrp AS targets.
source: Despite the absence of major changes in gene expression of other splicing factors, it is likely that other splicing factors contribute to the regulation of Esrp AS targets.
evidence: This is speculation based on the enrichment of other splicing factor motifs in the analysis.

claim: RBFOX2 has been shown to co-regulate ESRP AS events, including those associated with EMT, despite only small changes in RBFOX2 expression in EMT.
source: RBFOX2 has been shown to co-regulate ESRP AS events, including those associated with EMT, despite only small changes in RBFOX2 expression in EMT (Dittmar et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The ubiquitously expressed hnRNPM was shown to regulate splicing of CD44 during EMT, but only in conjunction with down regulation of the Esrps.
source: Similarly the ubiquitously expressed hnRNPM was shown to regulate splicing of CD44 during EMT, but only in conjunction with down regulation of the Esrps (Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The Esrps direct a program of AS that is highly conserved between human and mouse.
source: The Esrps direct a program of AS that is highly conserved between human and mouse and enriched in biologically coherent pathways involved in epithelial cell biology and function.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of human and mouse Esrp targets from previous studies.

claim: The Esrps are enriched in biologically coherent pathways involved in epithelial cell biology and function.
source: The Esrps direct a program of AS that is highly conserved between human and mouse and enriched in biologically coherent pathways involved in epithelial cell biology and function.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology and pathway analysis of Esrp targets.

claim: The Esrps are highly conserved in the three RRMs in the orthologous Fusilli in fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster) and Sym-2 in round worm (Caenorhabditis elegans).
source: The Esrps are also highly conserved in the three RRMs in the orthologous Fusilli in fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster) and Sym-2 in round worm (Caenorhabditis elegans).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison and established knowledge of protein conservation.

claim: Fusilli is partially functional in directing ESRP splicing events when transfected in human cells lacking the ESRPs.
source: We have shown that Fusilli is partially functional in directing ESRP splicing events when transfected in human cells lacking the ESRPs, indicating clear conservation of function (Warzecha et al., 2009a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The expression of Fusilli is epithelial-specific.
source: The expression of Fusilli is also epithelial-specific and both Fusilli and Sym-2 have been shown to function as a regulator of endogenous AS in Drosophila cells and C. elegans, respectively (Wakabayashi-Ito et al., 2001; Barberan-Soler and Zahler, 2008) (unpublished data).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and unpublished data.

claim: Both Fusilli and Sym-2 have been shown to function as a regulator of endogenous AS in Drosophila cells and C. elegans, respectively.
source: The expression of Fusilli is also epithelial-specific and both Fusilli and Sym-2 have been shown to function as a regulator of endogenous AS in Drosophila cells and C. elegans, respectively (Wakabayashi-Ito et al., 2001; Barberan-Soler and Zahler, 2008) (unpublished data).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In Drosophila, Fusilli homozygous mutation was lethal.
source: In Drosophila, Fusilli homozygous mutation was lethal, indicating that Esrp and Fusilli are both essential splicing factors despite substantial phylogenetic distance between mammals and flies.
evidence: This is based on unpublished data mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Esrp and Fusilli are both essential splicing factors despite substantial phylogenetic distance between mammals and flies.
source: In Drosophila, Fusilli homozygous mutation was lethal, indicating that Esrp and Fusilli are both essential splicing factors despite substantial phylogenetic distance between mammals and flies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lethality of both Esrp and Fusilli mutations.

claim: The increase in EDC gene expression in the DKO epidermis is likely an indirect effect of the loss of the Esrps.
source: The increase in EDC gene expression in the DKO epidermis is likely an indirect effect of the loss of the Esrps, but in turn it implicates Esrp regulated splicing in the maintenance of epithelial cell function necessary for barrier function in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with other barrier defect models and the mechanism of EDC gene regulation.

claim: The increase in EDC gene expression implicates Esrp regulated splicing in the maintenance of epithelial cell function necessary for barrier function in vivo.
source: The increase in EDC gene expression in the DKO epidermis is likely an indirect effect of the loss of the Esrps, but in turn it implicates Esrp regulated splicing in the maintenance of epithelial cell function necessary for barrier function in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that EDC gene upregulation is associated with barrier defects.

claim: Conditional ablation of Nf2 using Krt14-Cre resulted in mice with dry, flaky skin, and epidermal barrier defects as measured by water loss assay.
source: Similar to our Krt14-DKO mice, conditional ablation of Nf2 using Krt14-Cre resulted in mice with dry, flaky skin, and epidermal barrier defects as measured by water loss assay.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge from published literature about Nf2 conditional knockout.

claim: Nf2 was identified as an interaction partner with the adherens junction (AJ) and Par3 necessary for the maturation of AJ to mature TJs.
source: Biochemical evaluation identified Nf2 as an interaction partner with the adherens junction (AJ) and Par3 necessary for the maturation of AJ to mature TJs (Gladden et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The Esrps directly regulate the levels of Grhl1 by promoting exon 5 inclusion and preventing transcript degradation by NMD.
source: The Esrps directly regulate the levels of Grhl1 by promoting exon 5 inclusion and preventing transcript degradation by NMD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing splicing changes and transcript level changes for Grhl1.

claim: Mice lacking Grhl1 have reduced expression of desmosomal cadherins resulting in mild anchoring defects of hair follicles in the skin.
source: Mice lacking Grhl1 have reduced expression of desmosomal cadherins resulting in mild anchoring defects of hair follicles in the skin (Wilanowski et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Epidermal barrier defects by way of epidermal hyperplasia and inflammatory cell infiltration were observed in adult mice lacking Grhl1.
source: Epidermal barrier defects by way of epidermal hyperplasia and inflammatory cell infiltration were observed in adult mice lacking Grhl1 (Mlacki et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mice lacking Cd44 have delays in outside-in barrier formation during embryonic development and barrier formation measured in cultured keratinocytes.
source: Mice lacking Cd44, which in the case of the epidermis is the Esrp regulated epithelial form Cd44v, have delays in outside-in barrier formation during embryonic development and barrier formation measured in cultured keratinocytes (Kirschner et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: These examples of Esrp splicing targets involved in skin barrier function highlight the roles of the Esrps in regulating known genes involved in this process.
source: These examples of Esrp splicing targets involved in skin barrier function highlight the roles of the Esrps in regulating known genes involved in this process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that several Esrp targets are known barrier genes.

claim: Numerous Esrp-regulated targets will be shown to play roles in epithelial barrier function in the skin and other epithelial populations.
source: We predict that numerous Esrp-regulated targets will also be shown to play roles in epithelial barrier function in the skin and other epithelial populations.
evidence: This is speculation about future findings based on the current data.

claim: The Esrp DKO mice can be used to evaluate isoform-specific functions of known barrier genes.
source: Thus, the Esrp DKO mice can be used to evaluate isoform-specific functions of known barrier genes, as well as identify novel genes involved in the maintenance of epithelial barrier function via functions of epithelial specific protein isoforms.
evidence: This is speculation about potential uses of the mouse model.

claim: The Esrp DKO mice can be used to identify novel genes involved in the maintenance of epithelial barrier function via functions of epithelial specific protein isoforms.
source: Thus, the Esrp DKO mice can be used to evaluate isoform-specific functions of known barrier genes, as well as identify novel genes involved in the maintenance of epithelial barrier function via functions of epithelial specific protein isoforms.
evidence: This is speculation about potential uses of the mouse model.

claim: The KO of the Esrp proteins in mice provides the first evidence for a requirement for these cell-type-specific splicing factors in embryonic development and epithelial cell functions.
source: The KO of the Esrp proteins in mice provides the first evidence for a requirement for these cell-type-specific splicing factors in embryonic development and epithelial cell functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fact that this is the first in vivo study of Esrp function.

claim: The identification of the Esrp regulated splicing program provides numerous examples of genes that merit further investigation into their developmental functions and contribution to human diseases such as CL/P and diseases associated with epithelial barrier defects.
source: The identification of the Esrp regulated splicing program provides numerous examples of genes that merit further investigation into their developmental functions and contribution to human diseases such as CL/P and diseases associated with epithelial barrier defects.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the findings for future research.

claim: The compilation of Esrp regulated in vivo splicing targets in tissue-specific epithelial populations will provide further insights into the posttranscriptional splicing networks in epithelial cells at play during development and organogenesis of various tissues.
source: The compilation of Esrp regulated in vivo splicing targets in tissue-specific epithelial populations will provide further insights into the posttranscriptional splicing networks in epithelial cells at play during development and organogenesis of various tissues.
evidence: This is speculation about the value of the dataset for future research.
